transcription.tex: \textbf{Prove that there is no greatest odd integer.}
Assume that there is a greatest odd integer, \(n\).
Then \(n+2\) is an odd integer which is larger than \(n\).\par This contradicts the assumption that \(n\) is the greatest odd integer.
Therefore, there is no greatest odd integer.

\textbf{How to structure/word proof}\par “Assume that [negation of statement].”\par [Reasoning followed by…] “This contradicts the assumption that…” or “This is a contradiction.”\par “Therefore [restate original statement].”\par \textbf{Proof by contradiction}\par Assume the statement is false. Prove this leads to a contradiction. The original statement must therefore be true.

transcription.tex: The first part of a proof by contradiction requires you to negate the original statement. What is the negation of each statement? Click to choose.
\textbf{There are infinitely many prime numbers.}
There are infinitely many non-prime (i.e. composite) numbers.
There are finitely many prime numbers.
There are finitely many non-composite numbers.
\textbf{All Popes are Catholic.}
There exists a Pope who is not Catholic.
No Popes are Catholic.
Your Teacher is the Pope.
\textbf{If it is raining, my garden is wet.}
It is not raining and my garden is dry.
It is not raining and my garden is wet.
It is raining and my garden is not wet.
The negation of “all are” is “not all are”, not “none are”. For example, “not everyone likes green”. Do not confuse negation with an opposite.
The negation of “if A then B” is “A and not B”: the condition is true but the conclusion is false.

transcription.tex: Prove by contradiction that if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) must be even.
Assume there exists a number \(n\) such that \(n^2\) is even, but \(n\) is not even.

\(n\) is odd, therefore \(n=2k+1\) for some integer \(k\).\[\begin{aligned}n^2&=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1\\&=2(2k^2+2k)+1,\end{aligned}\]which is odd.\par This contradicts the assumption that \(n^2\) is even.
Therefore if \(n^2\) is even then \(n\) must be even.
\textbf{Negating a conditional statement}\par The negation of “if A then B” is “A and not B”.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Prove by contradiction that \(\sqrt2\) is an irrational number.
Assume that \(\sqrt2\) is a rational number.

Then \(\sqrt2=\dfrac ab\), where \(a,b\) are integers, \(b\ne0\), and the fraction is in its simplest form.\[2=\frac{a^2}{b^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 2b^2=a^2.\]Thus \(a^2\) is even, so \(a\) is even. Write \(a=2k\), where \(k\) is an integer.\[2b^2=(2k)^2=4k^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad b^2=2k^2.\]Thus \(b^2\) is even, so \(b\) is even. Both \(a\) and \(b\) are even, contradicting that \(a/b\) is in its simplest form.
Therefore \(\sqrt2\) is irrational.

\textbf{Rational and irrational numbers}\par A rational number can be expressed as \(a/b\), with integers \(a,b\) and \(b\ne0\). An irrational number cannot: examples include \(\pi,e,\sqrt3\).\par Rational numbers: \(\mathbb Q\); real numbers: \(\mathbb R\); natural numbers: \(\mathbb N\); integers: \(\mathbb Z\).\par \textbf{Alternative proof}\par In \(2b^2=a^2\), the power of 2 in the prime factorisation is odd on the left and even on the right. This is a contradiction.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Assume that there is a finite number of prime numbers.

List all the primes as \(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n\). Consider\[N=p_1p_2\cdots p_n+1.\]Division of \(N\) by any listed prime leaves remainder 1, so none of them divides \(N\).\par Either \(N\) is prime itself, or its prime factorisation contains primes not in the list. This contradicts the assumption that the list contains all primes.
Therefore, there are an infinite number of primes.
\textbf{Euclid’s proof}\par This is one of the earliest known proofs.\par Each stage can be revealed separately: assumption, contradiction, then conclusion.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{5(a)} Prove that if \(ab\) is irrational, then at least one of \(a,b\) is irrational. (3 marks)

Assume \(ab\) is irrational but both \(a,b\) are rational. Write\[a=\frac cd,\qquad b=\frac ef,\]where \(c,d,e,f\) are integers and \(d,f\ne0\). Then\[ab=\frac{ce}{df}\]is rational, since \(ce,df\) are integers and \(df\ne0\). This contradicts the assumption.\par Therefore at least one of \(a,b\) is irrational.
\textbf{5(b)} Prove that if \(a+b\) is irrational, then at least one of \(a,b\) is irrational. (3 marks)

Assume \(a+b\) is irrational but both \(a,b\) are rational. Write\[a=\frac cd,\qquad b=\frac ef,\]where \(c,d,e,f\) are integers and \(d,f\ne0\). Then\[a+b=\frac{cf+de}{df}\]is rational. This contradicts the assumption.\par Therefore at least one of \(a,b\) is irrational.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{6.} Use proof by contradiction to show that there exist no integers \(a,b\) for which \(21a+14b=1\).

Assume there exist integers \(a,b\) such that \(21a+14b=1\). Dividing by 7 gives\[3a+2b=\frac17.\]Since \(3a\) and \(2b\) are integers, their sum is an integer. But \(1/7\) is not an integer: a contradiction.\par Therefore there are no integers \(a,b\) for which \(21a+14b=1\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{7(a)} Prove by contradiction that if \(n^2\) is a multiple of 3, \(n\) is a multiple of 3. (3 marks)\par \textbf{7(b)} Hence prove by contradiction that \(\sqrt3\) is irrational. (3 marks)

\textbf{Part (a)} Assume \(n^2\) is a multiple of 3 but \(n\) is not. Then \(n=3k+1\) or \(n=3k+2\) for an integer \(k\).\[\begin{aligned}(3k+1)^2&=9k^2+6k+1=3(3k^2+2k)+1,\\(3k+2)^2&=9k^2+12k+4=3(3k^2+4k+1)+1.\end{aligned}\]In either case the square has remainder 1 on division by 3. This contradicts the assumption that \(n^2\) is a multiple of 3.\par Therefore, if \(n^2\) is a multiple of 3, so is \(n\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{7(a)} Prove by contradiction that if \(n^2\) is a multiple of 3, \(n\) is a multiple of 3. (3 marks)\par \textbf{7(b)} Hence prove by contradiction that \(\sqrt3\) is irrational. (3 marks)

\textbf{Part (b)} Assume \(\sqrt3=a/b\) for integers \(a,b\), with \(b\ne0\), in simplest terms. Then\[3=\frac{a^2}{b^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad a^2=3b^2.\]By part (a), \(a\) is a multiple of 3. Write \(a=3c\), where \(c\) is an integer.\[9c^2=3b^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad b^2=3c^2.\]By part (a), \(b\) is also a multiple of 3. Thus \(a,b\) have a common factor of 3, contradicting the fraction being in simplest terms.\par Therefore \(\sqrt3\) is irrational.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{8.} Use proof by contradiction to prove: “There are no integer solutions to \(x^2-y^2=2\).”

Assume there is an integer solution. Then \((x-y)(x+y)=2\). The integer factor pairs of 2 give:\[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x-y&x+y&x&y\\\hline2&1&3/2&-1/2\\1&2&3/2&1/2\\-2&-1&-3/2&1/2\\-1&-2&-3/2&-1/2\end{array}\]None gives integer values of \(x,y\), contradicting the assumption.\par Therefore there are no integer solutions to \(x^2-y^2=2\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{9.} Prove by contradiction that \(\sqrt[3]2\) is irrational.

Assume \(\sqrt[3]2=a/b\), where \(a,b\) are integers, \(b\ne0\), and the fraction is in simplest terms. Then \(a^3=2b^3\), so \(a^3\) is even and hence \(a\) is even. Write \(a=2n\), where \(n\) is an integer.\[\begin{aligned}(2n)^3&=2b^3,\\8n^3&=2b^3,\\b^3&=4n^3.\end{aligned}\]Thus \(b^3\) is even, so \(b\) is even too. This gives a common factor of 2, contradicting that \(a/b\) is in simplest terms.\par Therefore \(\sqrt[3]2\) is irrational.

transcription.tex: A number \(x\) is rational if \(x=m/n\) for integers \(m,n\) with \(n\ne0\). An irrational number cannot be written this way.
\textbf{A.} If \(pq\) is irrational, at least one of \(p,q\) is irrational.
Assume \(pq\) is irrational but \(p,q\) are both rational. Their product is then rational, contradicting the assumption. Therefore A is true.
\textbf{B.} If \(p+q\) is irrational, at least one of \(p,q\) is irrational.
Assume \(p+q\) is irrational but \(p,q\) are both rational. Their sum is then rational, contradicting the assumption. Therefore B is true.
\textbf{C.} Disprove: if \(p,q\) are irrational, then \(p+q\) is irrational.
Take \(p=\sqrt2\) and \(q=-\sqrt2\). Both are irrational, but \(p+q=0\) is rational. This is a counterexample.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Assuming \(e,\pi,\pi^2,e^2,e\pi\) are irrational, prove that at most one of \(\pi+e,\pi-e,\pi^2-e^2,\pi^2+e^2\) is rational.

\textbf{First rule out pairs}\par \((\pi+e)+(\pi-e)=2\pi\) is irrational, so \(\pi+e\) and \(\pi-e\) cannot both be rational.\par \((\pi^2+e^2)+(\pi^2-e^2)=2\pi^2\) is irrational, so these two cannot both be rational.\par If \(\pi+e\) and \(\pi^2-e^2\) were rational, then\[\pi-e=\frac{\pi^2-e^2}{\pi+e}\]would be rational, a contradiction. Similarly, \(\pi-e\) and \(\pi^2-e^2\) cannot both be rational.

\textbf{The remaining possible pairs}\par If two were rational, they would have to be \(\pi^2+e^2\) and one of \(\pi\pm e\).\par If \(\pi+e\) and \(\pi^2+e^2\) were rational, then\[2e\pi=(\pi+e)^2-(\pi^2+e^2)\]would be rational, contradicting the assumption.\par If \(\pi-e\) and \(\pi^2+e^2\) were rational, then\[2e\pi=(\pi^2+e^2)-(\pi-e)^2\]would be rational, again a contradiction.\par Therefore at most one of the four numbers is rational.

transcription.tex: To add or subtract fractions, find a common denominator.\par Simplify \(\dfrac3{x+1}-\dfrac2{x+2}\) and \(\dfrac3{x+1}-\dfrac{4x}{x^2-1}\).

\[\begin{aligned}\frac3{x+1}-\frac2{x+2}&=\frac{3(x+2)-2(x+1)}{(x+1)(x+2)}\\&=\frac{x+4}{(x+1)(x+2)}.\end{aligned}\]\par First look for common factors in the denominators to avoid unnecessary multiplication:\[\begin{aligned}\frac3{x+1}-\frac{4x}{x^2-1}&=\frac{3(x-1)-4x}{(x+1)(x-1)}\\&=\frac{-x-3}{(x+1)(x-1)}.\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: Given that\[\frac{6x^2+5x-2}{x(x-1)(2x+1)}\equiv\frac Ax+\frac B{x-1}+\frac C{2x+1},\]find \(A,B,C\).

Clear the denominators:\[6x^2+5x-2\equiv A(x-1)(2x+1)+Bx(2x+1)+Cx(x-1).\]\par Put \(x=1\): \(9=3B\Rightarrow B=3\).\par Put \(x=-\tfrac12\): \(-3=\tfrac34C\Rightarrow C=-4\).\par Put \(x=0\): \(-2=-A\Rightarrow A=2\).\[\frac{6x^2+5x-2}{x(x-1)(2x+1)}\equiv\frac2x+\frac3{x-1}-\frac4{2x+1}.\]

If \[\frac{x^2+5x-9}{x+2}=Ax+B+\frac C{x+2},\]determine \(A,B,C\).

\textbf{Algebraic division}\par The quotient has degree \(2-1=1\), so it has the form \(Ax+B\).\par \[\begin{array}{r}x^2+5x-9\\-(x^2+2x)\\\hline3x-9\\-(3x+6)\\\hline-15\end{array}\]\par Quotient: \(x+3\). Remainder: \(-15\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{7.} By factorising the denominator, express each fraction in partial fractions.

The denominator is \(x(x-2)^2\). Division gives\[x+\frac{5x^2-17x+12}{x(x-2)^2}.\]\par Write \(5x^2-17x+12\equiv A(x-2)^2+Bx(x-2)+Cx\).\par At \(x=0\): \(12=4A\Rightarrow A=3\).\par At \(x=2\): \(-2=2C\Rightarrow C=-1\).\par Compare \(x^2\): \(5=A+B\Rightarrow B=2\).\[x+\frac3x+\frac2{x-2}-\frac1{(x-2)^2}.\]
